title: Effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort
research_question: To examine the effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort, specifically: 1. quantify subjects' basic thermal comfort requirements in different seasons in the hot-humid climate of Taiwan; 2. determine whether subjects' thermal preferences can be effectively explained by heat-balance indices alone in different seasons; 3. determine the relative contributions of heat-balance parameters to thermal perception in an outdoor environment in different seasons.

participants.description: 1644 individuals from central Taiwan (Taichung, Yunlin, Chiayi) in outdoor environments. Data collected from winter 2004 to summer 2005.
participants.recruitment: Questionnaire surveys administered concurrently with physical microclimatic measurements as part of the FIOT project.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Outdoor environments in central Taiwan (Taichung, Yunlin, Chiayi) during hot (March-November) and cool (December-February) seasons. Micrometeorological parameters (Air temperature (Ta), Relative humidity (RH), Vapour pressure (VP), Air speed (v), Global solar radiation (G), Globe temperature (Tg), Mean radiant temperature (Tmrt)) were measured at waist height (1.1m).

mechanisms: Thermal adaptation: people take spontaneous behavioural actions (e.g., adjusting clothing) and psychological adjustments (e.g., differentiation of seasonal comfort expectations) to maintain thermal comfort across seasons.

Semantic artifact hypothesis: people may describe their preferred thermal state with different adjectives in different seasons (e.g., 'slightly cool' in summer vs. 'slightly warm' in winter), leading to discrepancies between neutral and preferred temperatures.
Previous experience: subjects' preferences for wind and humidity are influenced by their past experiences of how these factors help eliminate discomfort.
implementation_implications: The results can contribute to the planning and design of outdoor environments in hot-humid regions to support the use of outdoor spaces and increase occupant satisfaction.
A reasonable hot season design temperature range for outdoor recreational and sporting facilities in central Taiwan is about 29°C operative temperature.
An acceptable temperature range for Taiwan's cool season is 23.7-29.7°C.
If meteorological observations exceed acceptable ranges in the hot season, more shade should be provided to reduce Tmrt.
Elevated air speeds may be effective in bringing unacceptably high temperatures back into the acceptable range of 26-31°C in summer.

tables.description: Relative contribution of micrometeorological parameters (Operative temperature, Vapour pressure, Wind speed) to the explained variance in Thermal Sensation Vote (TSV) for hot and cool seasons.

limitations: The semantic artifact hypothesis may not be applicable to findings in central Taiwan, possibly because the contrast among seasons in Taiwan is not as great as in mid-latitude climate zones for which the hypothesis was originally proposed.
The study did not attempt to fit an acceptability range around preferred temperatures, but rather estimated it based on earlier comfort research (de Dear and Brager, 1998).

paper_metadata.title: Effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: AbstractThermal perceptions and preferences of individuals outdoors cannot be entirely explained by the energy balance of the human body. They are also affected by psychological and behavioural factors or the so‐called thermal adaptation. To examine the effect of thermal adaptation on seasonal outdoor thermal comfort, 1644 interviews with concurrent micrometeorological measurements were conducted outdoors in central Taiwan. Results indicate a deviation of 1.3 °C standard effective temperature (SET*) in neutral temperatures between hot and cool seasons, and a deviation of 1.8 °C SET* in preferred temperature between hot and cool seasons. Additionally, although subjects' temperature and sunshine preferences were highly correlated with SET*, they diverged between seasons for identical SET* exposures in the two seasons. Analysis reveals that people's thermal perceptions were strongly related to the air temperature (Ta) and mean radiant temperature (Tmrt), but not significant to air speed and air humidity. These results demonstrate that thermal adaptation markedly influences seasonal outdoor thermal comfort, knowledge of which may be useful in the planning and design of outdoor environments in hot–humid regions. Copyright © 2010 Royal Meteorological Society

theory_commitments.specific_claim: Human thermal comfort is not static but adapts to prevailing environmental conditions and past thermal experiences, leading to different comfort expectations across seasons and climates.

mechanism_chain.description: Individuals adjust their clothing insulation in response to perceived changes in outdoor air temperature to maintain thermal comfort, a key aspect of behavioral thermal adaptation.
